mismatches.patientClaim: Patient initially implies and pharmacy refills look consistent with full adherence, but patient eventually admits he intentionally skips the second dose some days when feeling well, in addition to forgetting after work.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows on-time monthly fills of 60 tablets (consistent with full 30-day BID supply) with no gaps - refill pattern alone looks perfect and would not reveal the 2-3x/week missed-dose pattern the patient admits to verbally.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Pharmacy refill/fill-date data can look reassuring (right quantity, right interval) while still masking real day-to-day non-adherence; refill history is a poor substitute for direct, non-judgmental adherence conversation, especially for twice-daily DOACs with short half-lives where missed doses meaningfully raise recurrence risk.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient describes the pink urine as a single, seemingly minor one-time event he dismissed and did not report to anyone.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Urinalysis ordered this visit shows persistent microscopic hematuria (15-20 RBC/hpf, flagged H) weeks after the described single visible episode, indicating ongoing bleeding rather than a resolved one-off event.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient-perceived 'one-time' bleeding symptoms can reflect ongoing, clinically significant bleeding; new hematuria in an anticoagulated patient always warrants objective testing and, if confirmed, urologic work-up to exclude an underlying structural lesion rather than being attributed to the anticoagulant alone.

objectives.text: Elicit and weigh risk factors (unprovoked proximal DVT, male sex, family history) that favor extended/indefinite anticoagulation over stopping at 3 months.
Identify clinically significant bleeding symptoms (recurrent epistaxis, bruising, and new hematuria) through sensitive, non-judgmental questioning, recognizing these were not previously volunteered.
Recognize and address a real-world adherence problem (missed/intentionally skipped doses) despite reassuring pharmacy refill data, understanding the limits of refill history as an adherence measure.

Correctly counsel that new hematuria in an anticoagulated patient requires objective testing and urology referral/work-up rather than attribution to anticoagulation alone, staying within hematology scope by coordinating referral rather than managing the urologic cause directly.

Explain appropriately that thrombophilia testing in this setting would not change the anticoagulation decision and discuss its limitations (timing, effect of anticoagulation on results, lack of actionable change in management for an unprovoked proximal DVT already favoring extended therapy).
Interpret D-dimer drawn while on anticoagulation correctly as uninterpretable for off-treatment recurrence risk stratification.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Unprovoked proximal (femoropopliteal) DVT in a man with new bleeding symptoms (epistaxis, hematuria) and partial medication non-adherence, presenting for a decision about extended anticoagulation.
differential: Continue indefinite/extended anticoagulation given unprovoked proximal DVT with strong family history (favored)
Stop anticoagulation at standard 3-month course (not favored given unprovoked nature, male sex, family history)
Underlying unrecognized thrombophilia (testing would not change current management)
Bleeding attributable to apixaban alone (possible but new hematuria requires exclusion of a structural urologic cause before attribution)
Post-thrombotic syndrome contributing to residual leg swelling (supportive care, not a reason to stop anticoagulation)
keyFindings: Unprovoked left common femoral/femoral/popliteal DVT 3 months ago, no identifiable provoking factor
Strong family history: father with PE at 45, paternal aunt with pregnancy-associated VTE, neither genetically tested

Residual left leg swelling worse by evening, calf circumference asymmetry (left 39 cm vs right 36.5 cm in the evening); this diurnal pattern and degree of asymmetry has been essentially stable over the past 3 weeks per home log, which is reassuring against new/worsening thrombus and more consistent with chronic post-thrombotic change
Admits missing apixaban doses 2-3 times/week despite pharmacy refill history looking fully adherent
New recurrent epistaxis (~weekly) and bruising on forearms not previously reported
New hematuria: one visible episode plus confirmed microscopic hematuria (15-20 RBC/hpf) on urinalysis, obtained once the patient disclosed the episode
D-dimer mildly elevated while on apixaban - not interpretable for off-anticoagulation recurrence risk
CBC and creatinine normal, apixaban dosing appropriate for renal function
plan: Recommend extended (indefinite) anticoagulation given unprovoked proximal DVT, male sex, and significant family history of VTE, pending shared decision-making discussion of ongoing bleeding risk vs recurrence risk

Address adherence directly and non-judgmentally: discuss barriers (fatigue after shifts, belief that occasional skipping is safe), consider reminder strategies/pillbox, reinforce that twice-daily dosing with short half-life means missed doses meaningfully raise recurrence risk

Elicit the hematuria history directly and sensitively, then order/confirm urinalysis; refer to urology for new hematuria work-up (confirmed microscopic hematuria plus one visible episode) rather than attributing to apixaban alone; do not stop anticoagulation solely for this without urology input unless bleeding becomes major or hemodynamically significant

Do not order thrombophilia panel at this time; explain to patient that results would not change the recommendation for extended anticoagulation and may be unreliable while on apixaban/soon after acute clot

Disregard D-dimer drawn on treatment for recurrence-risk decision-making; if an off-anticoagulation D-dimer strategy is ever considered in the future, it would need to be drawn after a trial period off anticoagulation, which is not being pursued here given risk profile

Counsel on compression stocking use and leg elevation for residual swelling/post-thrombotic symptoms; note that the swelling pattern has been stable for weeks, which is reassuring, and encourage more consistent stocking use with practical modifications for hot work environment
Advise on bleeding precautions: when to seek urgent care (heavy/uncontrollable bleeding, blood in stool, severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath)
Coordinate with primary care regarding ongoing monitoring and urology referral; schedule hematology follow-up in 4-6 weeks after urology evaluation and adherence reassessment
redFlags: New hematuria in an anticoagulated patient requires prompt objective testing and urology referral to exclude a structural lesion (e.g., malignancy) rather than attribution to the anticoagulant alone
Recurrent epistaxis and easy bruising raise bleeding risk that must be weighed against recurrence risk, but are not yet major bleeding
Any new chest pain, dyspnea, or hemoptysis would need urgent escalation for possible recurrent PE (currently absent)
Severe or worsening leg swelling with pain/warmth would need re-evaluation for DVT extension or recurrence (current swelling pattern is stable over 3 weeks, which is reassuring)
educationPoints: Unprovoked proximal (femoropopliteal) DVT in men carries a higher recurrence risk than distal or provoked clots, generally favoring extended or indefinite anticoagulation after shared decision-making about bleeding risk
D-dimer measured while a patient is still anticoagulated does not reliably predict recurrence risk off treatment and should not be used to decide whether to stop therapy

Thrombophilia testing rarely changes management in a patient who already has a clear indication for extended anticoagulation based on clinical risk factors (unprovoked proximal DVT, family history), and results can be altered by concurrent anticoagulation or by testing too soon after the acute event

Pharmacy refill timing/quantity data can look perfectly adherent while missing real-world missed or intentionally skipped doses; direct, non-judgmental adherence conversations are essential, especially for short-half-life twice-daily DOACs

New bleeding symptoms such as hematuria in an anticoagulated patient should prompt a search for an underlying structural cause rather than being dismissed as an expected anticoagulant side effect, and must be actively elicited since patients may not spontaneously report a seemingly minor one-time episode

Family history of VTE (especially in a first-degree relative with PE at a young age) strengthens, but does not by itself confirm, an inherited thrombophilia, and does not need to be proven by genetic testing to influence the duration-of-anticoagulation decision in this patient

Stable, longstanding diurnal leg swelling asymmetry should be distinguished from new or worsening swelling; a stable pattern over weeks is reassuring and more consistent with chronic post-thrombotic change than with clot extension or recurrence

profile.summary: A 38-year-old man with an unprovoked proximal DVT 3 months ago and a strong family history of VTE requests to stop apixaban, but the visit uncovers inconsistent adherence despite reassuring pharmacy refill data and new, unreported bleeding symptoms including hematuria that need urology referral. The case teaches extended-anticoagulation decision-making for unprovoked proximal DVT, the limits of D-dimer and thrombophilia testing while on treatment, and the gap between refill-based adherence metrics and real patient behavior.
